analysis.one_liner: Restores the overtime pay threshold for salaried workers to $47,476 and updates it every three years.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have extended overtime protections to millions of salaried workers, never received a committee hearing or a vote in the Senate.
analysis.plain_summary: Under federal law, most salaried workers earning above a certain amount can be denied overtime pay even when they work 60-hour weeks. In 2016, the Labor Department raised that cutoff from $23,660 a year to $47,476, which would have extended or strengthened overtime protection for about 13 million workers, but a federal court threw the rule out. This bill would have written that higher threshold directly into law and required automatic updates every three years so it could not fall out of date again.
analysis.who_benefits: Salaried workers earning between the old threshold ($23,660 a year) and the new one ($47,476 a year) — largely managers, supervisors, and office workers in retail, restaurants, and other industries — who would become newly eligible for time-and-a-half pay over 40 hours, or strengthened protection if already eligible. The bill's findings cite the 2016 rule as benefiting more than 13 million employees, including 4.2 million newly covered.

how_it_helps.text: Writes into the Fair Labor Standards Act a salary threshold equal to the 40th percentile of full-time salaried earnings in the lowest-wage Census region — $913 a week, or $47,476 a year — below which salaried workers cannot be denied overtime pay.

Adopts the 2016 Labor Department rule that the bill says would benefit more than 13 million employees: overtime protections for 4.2 million new workers and strengthened protections for 8.9 million more.

Requires the threshold to be automatically updated every three years based on current wage data, without needing a new rulemaking, so it does not erode again as the previous threshold did — the bill notes more than 60% of full-time salaried workers earned below the threshold in 1975 but under 7% did by 2016.
Leaves the old threshold of $455 a week ($23,660 a year) behind — an amount the bill notes was below the poverty line for a family of four.

analysis.who_pays: Employers who currently pay salaried workers between roughly $24,000 and $47,500 without overtime — especially retail and restaurant chains that run on long-hours, low-salary management jobs, plus smaller businesses with similar payrolls. They would pay overtime premiums, raise salaries above the threshold, or cap hours.

drawbacks.text: Employers would face higher labor costs: overtime premiums, salary raises to keep workers exempt, or limits on how many hours salaried staff can work — costs that could be passed to consumers or reduce staffing flexibility.
Some salaried workers value flexibility and would be shifted to hourly tracking of their time, and businesses would face new compliance and recordkeeping burdens.

The jump from a $23,660 threshold to $47,476 was large — roughly double — and the threshold formula tied to the lowest-wage region drew criticism that it was set too high for lower-cost parts of the country.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core tradeoff is a straightforward one: workers who now put in unpaid overtime get paid for it, and the employers who benefit from those unpaid hours pay for it. The threshold the bill adopts is actually lower than several alternatives it lays out (including the inflation-adjusted $51,168 and the 1975-equivalent $58,344), which supports its claim to be a measured increase. The main honest objection is the transition cost to employers, particularly small businesses, and the loss of scheduling flexibility for some newly hourly workers — but the automatic three-year update fixes a real, documented problem with the old system.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate committee that handles labor law, and the committee never took it up, so it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Sherrod Brown introduced the bill on November 30, 2017, joined by 12 Democratic cosponsors, all senators.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where no further action was recorded before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

The bill was written to restore the 2016 Labor Department overtime rule raising the exemption threshold to $47,476 a year, after a federal district court in Texas invalidated that rule, which the bill's findings say threatened overtime protections for millions of workers.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who pay long-hours salaried managers under $47,500 avoided a legal requirement to pay them overtime. Workers who would have gained overtime protection got nothing, and the threshold stayed at $23,660 a year for the life of the Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who avoided the higher overtime threshold

for.name: Sen. Sherrod Brown
for.role: U.S. Senator from Ohio, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Restoring Overtime Pay Act and gathered 12 Senate cosponsors.

for.name: 12 Democratic senators
for.role: Original cosponsors, including Sen. Patty Murray (the ranking member of the labor committee) and Sens. Warren, Gillibrand, Durbin, Booker, and others

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Lamar Alexander
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no vote — during the remainder of the 115th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican support is recorded; the bill never advanced past its committee referral.

industries.note: These industries rely heavily on salaried store and shift managers earning between $24,000 and $47,500 who routinely work long hours without overtime. The bill would have required overtime pay or salary raises for that workforce, directly converting employer cost into worker pay.

Any business with salaried staff below the threshold would face new overtime or salary costs and compliance work. The impact varies widely by pay structure, and workers at these firms would share in the benefit.
